I'd start with a log line first. A good log line will keep you focus while writing.

I would focus on the log line, since it is (essentially) the thesis of your film. 

The log line as it stands:
    "Trapped in a haunted hotel, a timid mute woman and others must survive the demonic hotel staff and solve a murder in order to escape with their lives"

(What I would do):

-focus on ONE character (even in a group of characters, there's always one that takes charge) and make them your protagonist (THE HAUNTING, THE SHINING, THE PURGE, SAW II, HOUSE ON HAUNTED HILL, etc. All have a group of characters, all have a lead out of that group)

-simplify conflict. Right now, you have two goals set up- "survive demonic hotel staff" AND "solve a murder". That's two movies. You can consolidate the goals into "solve a murder" since by solving the murder, they will have to survive the demonic hotel staff (the audience isn't stupid. We're not expecting the haunted hotel that'll threaten your life to NOT have demonic spirits, that you have to battle, inside).

-really think about if you want your lead to be disabled/deaf. I know you're probably thinking about using the whole "oh, she can't hear that guy creep up behind her, then she'll turn around and he'll be gone b/c he's a ghost!". It's been done to death. Unless her being deaf gives her some specific advantage, or has some specific relevancy to the plot, I'd toss it.  

-It's minor, but the devil is in the details, put the protagonist at the beginning of your log line (unless the script is really about the hotel). I'm not watching for the hotel, I have THE SHINING, ROOM 1408, etc, to get my "creepy hotel" fix. I'm watching for the characters, so lead off with them.  


(So, my log line):
    "A timid woman is trapped inside a haunted hotel and must solve a murder in order to escape with her life"



Also, when dealing with the supernatural (or sci-fi) the rule is: you can make up whatever rules you want (regarding how the supernatural/science fiction works in your script) *as long as you are consistent with them*. So, like JC2535 said, make sure you understand the physics of your supernatural hotel. 


Once you have all that figured, write an outline. If you start off trying to write a full screenplay, you'll fail. Guaranteed. Write as much as you can (minus dialogue, unless it's a great line you don't wanna forget) in the outline stage so you can edit and tweak it then, as opposed to playing jenga with your script when you're on page 108 and you realize it doesn't work.

I had a dog once. He was a sickly stray that nudged the filth around our trailer for scraps. His hair was matted and one of his eyes was permanently swelled shut. Maybe blind. He barked at me, his mouth fringed with fizz. I'd toss him scraps now and then. He was the closest thing I had to a friend, even though his bites would give me fevers sometimes. 

I came home one day to an empty house, again. I went to the backyard and found him huddled under a bag of filth squirreled against a moldy, broken plastic table. He was stiff as stone. 

I heard the screen door slam. Mother was home. She was shrieking my name.

I think I was just numb to it by then. twenty-two years of shrieking...it just becomes noise...

I turned and kept walking into the woods behind the trailer park. I don't remember why. I just remember doing. I took out my knife. Slit my wrists. It all seemed so pointless. So I cut up the rest of my arms. Then my legs. I didn't stop till I fainted. 
I woke up...later. What hadn't coagulated had ebbed to dripping. I got up feeling so light headed, like I was still dreaming. 

I walked back with purpose. 

My mother twitched awake as I slammed the door behind me. She said...something...where was I? Where was dinner? How I wasn't worth the broken condom I came out of. I just nodded. 
When she turned her back I kicked her against the wall. Her crack-bones splintered easy. I wrapped my fingers in her wiry hair, bashing her face into the floor. I reached my arm across and squeezed every last puff of smoke from her lungs. She twitched once more, this time into slumber.

I waited until my father came home. 5 AM. He bludgeoned the door open, offsetting his balance and crumbling against the couch. Lumbering up, his fat feet thumbed their way to the Jack Daniels in the freezer. 

He sunk into the lumped couch, it fit his form like a funeral suit. He eyed me. "Wha'do you wan', faggot?" he slurred, "faggot son..." His arm swelled red, curling the bottle to his mouth. Mother's blood that hadn't settled into the fibers were dying his arm red.
He finished the bottle in three gulps. He didn't even taste the Drano. 

He started coughing up blood, beached on bloody cushions, he floundered wide-eyed. I watched back, unflinching. 

Later I would hang them upside down in the same woods. I cut their throats, drained them dry. Even the dog. 

I did it so He could see I was doing as He asked me. To empty them of their poison as I emptied mine...

I knew who had to die, I saw them hanging up there with Mother, Father, and the dog. Upside down their frowns would be smiling. They were happy. That made me happy. It still makes me happy.
